title: Deity yoga, explained
hook: visualizing oneself as an awakened figure, understood as empty and luminous

segments.voice: Yesterday, guru yoga, the last of the four foundations. Your line was joining minds. Whose hands were moving when you did that one thing? Day one thousand three hundred nine.

What comes up when you picture yourself? For some people it's someone a little tired, a little behind, with a list of flaws ready to recite. A picture like that can run all day, mostly unnoticed, shaping what seems possible. Tibetan tantric Buddhism looks at that habit and does something bold with it. It doesn't argue with the old picture. It replaces it, on purpose, for the length of a meditation, with the picture of an awakened being. To an outsider it can look like pretending. Today, what it actually is.
screen: `THE PICTURE YOU CARRY OF YOURSELF.` → `IT RUNS ALL DAY.` → `REPLACE IT, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, what deity yoga is. In Vajrayana, the practitioner visualizes themselves as an awakened figure, such as Tara or Avalokiteshvara, with a body made of light and the surroundings as a pure land. The deity isn't a god to be pleased from a distance. It's a form of awakening itself. Second, empty and luminous. The practice usually begins by letting the ordinary self-image dissolve into emptiness. Then the deity arises out of that emptiness, clear and vivid, but without any solid substance, like a rainbow or a reflection in a mirror. Teachers call that the guardrail. If the figure were solid, they say, this would just be a fancier ego. Because it's understood as empty, it loosens the grip of every self-image, the old one included. Third, two qualities Tibetan teachers name: clear appearance, seeing the form vividly, and what's often called divine pride, a steady confidence of being awakened that isn't the ego's pride at all. Fourth, how it's learned. In Tibetan traditions, full deity yoga is practiced after receiving empowerment and instruction from a qualified teacher, usually on the foundations you met this week. So this is an explanation, not the practice. And this week's road led here: one intention, morning and night. All the way down. The foundations. The whole world offered. Washed clean. Joining minds. Each one clears ground, so that seeing yourself as awakened rests on something real.
screen: `YOURSELF AS AN AWAKENED FIGURE.` · `ARISING FROM EMPTINESS, LIKE A RAINBOW.` · `CLEAR APPEARANCE, DIVINE PRIDE.` · `LEARNED WITH EMPOWERMENT AND A TEACHER.` · then, large: `AS THE DEITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture yourself as kindness. This isn't deity yoga, just a small taste of the idea, open to anyone. Sit and let the breath settle. Let your usual picture of yourself soften, the list and the flaws, like mist thinning. Then, for these two minutes, picture yourself made of kindness, clear as a reflection, with nothing solid to defend. Feel how that body would sit, how it would breathe, what it would do next. When thoughts of the old picture return, let them pass like weather. The bell holds the time.
Deity yoga. Seeing yourself as an awakened figure, understood as empty and luminous, like a rainbow. Today's word.
Your line: as the deity. Today, when the old picture of yourself starts its speech, ask once what the kind one would do next, and do it. Day one thousand three hundred nine.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners take up deity yoga after receiving empowerment and instruction from a teacher, typically meditating daily with a practice text in which they arise as the deity from emptiness and recite the deity's mantra.

original.note: Sanskrit devata: deity. Tibetan Buddhists use yidam for the deity a practitioner meditates on.
